chunks.content: 1 INTRODUCTION First‐trimester abortion is a common and safe procedure to terminate a pregnancy performed through two methods, medical (administration of mifepristone followed by misoprostol) or surgical (vacuum aspiration). In most European countries, more than 90% of abortions are performed before 13 weeks of amenorrhea and over two‐thirds of abortions are carried out before 9 weeks of amenorrhea. First‐trimester abortion is considered a low‐risk procedure, with a complication rate of less than 2% when performed by trained healthcare providers. Prevalence of the Rhesus (Rh)‐negative blood type varies significantly across the globe. It is most frequent among those of European and North American ancestry, where 15%–17% of people have the RhD‐negative phenotype. In comparison, the occurrence is lower in Africa and India, ranging from 3% to 8%, and exceedingly rare in Asia, with only 0.1%–0.3% of the population being Rh‐negative. , Determination of RhD status and the administration of immunoglobulin G (IgG) anti‐D prophylaxis to RhD‐negative women undergoing first‐trimester abortion, continues to be a subject of discussion and evolving practice within the field of reproductive health care. Historically, the clinical practice has been to routinely test for RhD status and administer IgG anti‐D to all non‐sensitized RhD‐negative women, regardless of their pregnancy term. In most cases, a full dose of IgG anti‐D is given, 250–300 μg (1250–1500 IU), which is sufficient to neutralize 30 mL of fetal blood in the women's blood circulation. , , This practice was deduced from the Rh alloimmunization risk caused by the feto‐maternal transfusion of RhD‐positive red blood cells (RBCs) during delivery, sensitizing the mother's immune system. This RhD alloimmunization can lead to life‐threatening complications for the fetus in subsequent pregnancies, such as hemolytic disease of the RhD‐positive newborn, and was therefore considered an important risk to mitigate. , , , However, in early pregnancy there are few if any fetal RBCs present with a questionable antigenic capacity. It is inherently difficult to study the potential impact of a small volume of fetal RBCs on the womans immune system. Consequently, the evidence about the need of anti‐D prophylaxis in first‐trimester abortion has been very limited and inconsistent. , , , Recent guidelines questioned routine RhD testing and IgG anti‐D administration for first‐trimester abortions, citing the low risk of RhD sensitization due to minimal fetal RBCs, along with potential drawbacks like increased costs, delays in care, and barriers to abortion access. , , , The negative impact of Rh testing is particularly significant in medical abortion as it becomes an increasingly self‐managed procedure. Blood typing and the administration of IgG are the only invasive interventions in an otherwise entirely oral treatment. Additionally, the introduction of medical abortion has led to a significant decrease in average gestational age at which abortions are performed in most countries. Consequently, the balance between benefits and potential risks of this practice had to be re‐evaluated ; also keeping in mind that the IgG are of human origin, derived from blood donors who were sensitized. As evidence evolves, it is crucial that healthcare providers stay informed on the latest recommendations and make accurate decisions based on reliable data, to ensure that the management of RhD status and anti‐D prophylaxis balance benefits and potential risks for each woman undergoing first‐trimester abortion. This review brings together and critically analyzes the existing guidelines on Rh testing and anti‐D prophylaxis in the context of first‐trimester abortion, alongside current literature supporting or opposing this practice to enable an informed decision‐making in clinical practice. 2 METHODOLOGY The present study is a systematic review based on a published protocol in PROSPERO (registration number: CRD42024544320). 2.1 Literature search Scientific articles were searched on MEDLINE/Pubmed, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, Google Scholar, and in the gray literature (such as health authorities' websites, patients' advocacy communication, learned societies communications) databases from January 1, 2003, to January 17, 2024. The search strategy was limited to articles published in English and French, on humans, and based on an algorithm with the combination of appropriate keywords and MESH terms. The search algorithm is provided in Data . 2.2 Study selection Two review authors (MC, A‐AV) conducted separate assessments of the relevance and eligibility of publications retrieved from the search algorithm. Initially, they assessed titles and abstracts, excluding any publications that did not meet the inclusion criteria. Subsequently, they independently evaluated the full texts of selected publications. Reasons for exclusion were clearly documented. A flowchart illustrating the study selection is available in Data . Various publication types were included to gain a comprehensive understanding of anti‐D prophylaxis practice during first‐trimester abortion, namely guidelines (international, national, and expert consensus), reviews, meta‐analyses, observational and qualitative studies, randomized controlled trials, cohort, and practice survey studies. Case studies and studies describing specific theoretical RhD management that have not been experimented or implemented in practice were excluded. RhD interventions related to induced abortion or

publications that did not meet the inclusion criteria. Subsequently, they independently evaluated the full texts of selected publications. Reasons for exclusion were clearly documented. A flowchart illustrating the study selection is available in Data . Various publication types were included to gain a comprehensive understanding of anti‐D prophylaxis practice during first‐trimester abortion, namely guidelines (international, national, and expert consensus), reviews, meta‐analyses, observational and qualitative studies, randomized controlled trials, cohort, and practice survey studies. Case studies and studies describing specific theoretical RhD management that have not been experimented or implemented in practice were excluded. RhD interventions related to induced abortion or miscarriage (spontaneous abortion) included were defined as: international and national guidelines or expert consensus on RhD testing and anti‐D prophylaxis, as well as any available literature or real‐world data assessing the management of anti‐D prophylaxis and collecting any evidence for RhD screening and anti‐D administration in RhD‐negative women undergoing first‐trimester abortion. The population of patients considered was restricted to adult women (≥18 years old) having an abortion/miscarriage during the first trimester. The outcomes considered were: Overview of existing guidelines of RhD testing and anti‐D prophylaxis (international, national, expert consensus, etc.) Advantages/disadvantages of RhD management in first‐trimester abortion Evidence for and/or against giving anti‐D prophylaxis in first‐trimester abortion. Table summarizes the inclusion and exclusion criteria used to select publications. For grey literature, relevant sources were included to complement peer‐reviewed studies and ensure a comprehensive understanding of current practices. These sources were identified through targeted searches of government agencies, public health institutions, professional societies, and conference materials. Eligible documents addressed RhD testing or anti‐D immunoglobulin administration in the context of early pregnancy loss, originated from recognized and credible organizations, and were publicly accessible with clear authorship and publication date. Recent and relevant documents were prioritized. Sources lacking methodologic transparency, clear scope, or originating from unvalidated sources were excluded. A narrative assessment of relevance and quality was applied, given the diversity of document types included in the review. 2.3 Data extraction A standardized extraction grid was used to extract information from the selected articles, regardless of study design, to ensure consistency and comparability. The grid was adapted to accommodate the varying scope and reporting formats of different study types. Although data completeness varied, all relevant information available was systematically recorded. The following information was extracted: Study characteristics (identification of the publication (first author, title, DOI), country, year of publication, year of the study, study design/type, number of individuals who participated in the study) Population characteristics (gestational age, type of pregnancy termination [threatened, spontaneous, induced surgical/medical abortion, miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy termination], RhD status, population source [registry, single‐center, multicenter, national or international], type of control group [none, standard of care, no intervention, other]) Characteristics of the intervention (objective of the intervention [RhD testing, anti‐D prophylaxis], gestational age for RhD testing, gestational age for anti‐D treatment, anti‐D dosage, patients' request considered in RhD prophylaxis administration [yes/no], location of intervention [city, hospital], providers [specialist doctor, general practitioner, nurse, psychologist, social assistance, other]) Results criteria (type of results: RhD alloimmunization, quality of life, patient satisfaction, and economic impact [individual, health system, or societal perspective], value of the result in the intervention arm, value of the result in the “no intervention” arm, level of significance of the comparison between the intervention and the no intervention arms). The information was extracted by the study investigators from January 2024 to March 2024, by reading the full text of each publication. The same two review authors (CM, A‐AV) were involved in the extraction data process: one reviewer extracted data, and the other checked. Any disagreements between individual judgments were resolved by consensus. Missing data were indicated as such. Data extractions were recorded in an Excel spreadsheet. 2.4 Risk of bias and quality assessment A narrative assessment of methodologic quality and potential bias was performed for all included sources (at study level), adapted to the type of publication. MC and A‐AV reviewers were involved in the quality assessment: one author assessed the studies' quality and the other checked the decision made. Any disagreements between individual judgments were resolved by consensus. Due to the heterogeneity of study designs, standardized bias assessment tools could not be uniformly applied. Key factors considered included study design, sample size, transparency in reporting, and, for guidelines, the declared level of supporting evidence. 2.5 Steering Committee involvement A Steering Committee, composed of experienced abortion care providers from nine European countries, was established to provide expert guidance throughout the project. The Committee validated the search strategy and keywords used in the literature review, reviewed the collected data, and offered expert interpretation on key topics. They also contributed to the development of consensus‐building themes to inform future clinical guidance on the management of RhD in the context of first‐trimester abortion. The Steering Committee's role was strictly advisory and scientific; they did not

The Committee validated the search strategy and keywords used in the literature review, reviewed the collected data, and offered expert interpretation on key topics. They also contributed to the development of consensus‐building themes to inform future clinical guidance on the management of RhD in the context of first‐trimester abortion. The Steering Committee's role was strictly advisory and scientific; they did not participate in patient recruitment or data collection, as the study did not involve the collection of individual patient data. 3 RESULTS 3.1 Study selection and characteristics A total of 609 references were gathered from the period covering January 1, 2003, to January 17, 2024: 279 from PubMed, 326 from EMBASE, and 4 from Cochrane Library. Among these, 27 publications met the inclusion criteria, with details of exclusions provided in Data . Additionally, 17 publications were sourced from the gray literature. A total of 44 studies were included in the analysis (Data ). The complete list of gray literature sources is provided in Data . The distribution of publications varied across the years, with the highest proportion published in 2022 (18%) (Table ). The geographical distribution of the studies shows a predominant focus on Europe (45%), particularly France and the UK (9% and 11%, respectively), followed by the Americas (27%), primarily the USA (16%) (Table ), reflecting the geographical distribution of Rh negativity. Some studies (23%) had an international scope (studies involving multiple countries from different continents). Most of the studies were guidelines (61%), followed by reviews (18%). Other types of articles, including expert consensus and surveys, represented smaller proportions and mainly revised and re‐analyzed already existing evidence (Table ). 3.2 Analysis of existing RhD guidelines in the context of abortion Table provides an overview of the 27 included guidelines regarding RhD practice across countries and organizations, categorized by the method of pregnancy termination and miscarriage addressed, including surgical and medical abortion. These guidelines, providing a comprehensive overview of RhD practice worldwide, incorporate data from various international bodies, such as FIGO (the International Federation of Gynecology & Obstetrics), the International Confederation of Midwives, and World Health Organization (WHO), as well as European countries (Austria, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, The Netherlands, Spain, and the UK), and Americas (Canada, USA, Mexico, and Colombia). Furthermore, guidelines from Australia and New Zealand are also featured. The analysis of RhD practices reveals a lack of evidence‐based data resulting in a significant variability in recommendations and approaches among the different countries. Notably, concerning RhD screening, while the latest international (WHO 2022 ), Australian , and Italian (Italian Superior Institute of Health recommendations on medical abortion) recommendations on abortion advise that it is not mandatory for women undergoing first‐trimester abortion, many recent guidelines recommend it during first‐trimester abortion. , , , , The recommended gestational age above which IgG anti‐D should be given to women who had an abortion is even more heterogeneous. Indeed, many European countries' recommendations were written before 2022 and recommend anti‐D prophylaxis for RhD‐negative women undergoing first‐trimester abortion, in particular Austria (>6 weeks of amenorrhea), the Netherlands (>7 weeks of amenorrhea), Germany (<9 weeks of amenorrhea), and Ireland (>10 weeks of amenorrhea). Conversely, international guidelines and some national guidelines (from WHO, National Abortion Federation [NAF], the USA, and the UK, Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists [RCOG] ), published in 2022 or after, suggest anti‐D prophylaxis for RhD‐negative women after 12 or more weeks of amenorrhea. The 2023 NICE (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence) guidelines recommend avoiding anti‐D prophylaxis for women undergoing solely medical management for an ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage, those with a threatened or complete miscarriage, or those with a pregnancy of unknown location. Similarly, the most recent recommendations from the Italian Superior Institute of Health advise against anti‐D prophylaxis for women undergoing medical abortion before 9 weeks of amenorrhea, except in cases with a high risk of feto‐maternal hemorrhage. In contrast, the guidelines from Spain, the Czech Republic, France, and Canada, published before 2022, recommend anti‐D prophylaxis for RhD‐negative women regardless of gestational age. Besides, the gestational age threshold may vary depending on the type of abortion, medical versus surgical, induced versus spontaneous. It has also been observed that the management of anti‐D prophylaxis has evolved over time, both internationally and within individual countries, such as the UK (Table ). Additionally, the consideration of patient informed consent for the administration of IgG anti‐D is not consistent across guidelines. Only some guidelines (8/27) specify the requirement for patient consent and its inclusion in the decision making process regarding IgG anti‐D administration (Table ). For guidelines recommending IgG anti‐D

for RhD‐negative women regardless of gestational age. Besides, the gestational age threshold may vary depending on the type of abortion, medical versus surgical, induced versus spontaneous. It has also been observed that the management of anti‐D prophylaxis has evolved over time, both internationally and within individual countries, such as the UK (Table ). Additionally, the consideration of patient informed consent for the administration of IgG anti‐D is not consistent across guidelines. Only some guidelines (8/27) specify the requirement for patient consent and its inclusion in the decision making process regarding IgG anti‐D administration (Table ). For guidelines recommending IgG anti‐D prophylaxis, dosage varies significantly, ranging from 50 μg for Czech Republic guidelines to 300 μg for Spanish and Canadian guidelines. The guidelines reviewed were predominantly based on studies with low‐quality evidence in the context of abortion. When the level of evidence was specified, it was consistently graded as moderate to low (Grade B or C), relying on randomized clinical trials with significant limitations, observational studies, or case series. 3.3 Evidence regarding <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">IgG</styled-content> anti‐D administration in first‐trimester abortion The heterogeneity in guidelines and practices regarding anti‐D prophylaxis in first‐trimester abortion is mainly due to the lack of evidence. Most guidelines therefore detract from recommendations during childbirth and are based on other factors: varying interpretations of few and weak evidence that is available, IgG anti‐D availability, historical, cultural and social factors, legal and regulatory considerations, pressure of the peer group, and evolving evidence. Table provides an overview of all arguments and evidence supporting and opposing the practice of IgG anti‐D prophylaxis in first‐trimester abortion, found in the literature. Various points and counterpoints regarding the administration of IgG anti‐D are present in the literature. Among the frequently cited arguments in favor are the reduction in anti‐RhD alloimmunization historically observed in European countries, , the prevention of RhD alloimmunization and associated risks in future pregnancies, , , and findings from a systematic review referenced by WHO indicating fewer instances of antibody formation in those given IgG anti‐D compared with those who were not, with no reported adverse effects , (Table ). Several studies highlight arguments against the routine use of IgG anti‐D. These include the lack of conclusive evidence of risk of RhD alloimmunization at early gestational ages, , , , , and findings suggesting that the risk of alloimmunization for RhD‐negative women with spontaneous abortion before 10 weeks of amenorrhea may be negligible or non‐existant. , Additionally, the latest WHO guidelines recommend against anti‐D prophylaxis for both medical and surgical abortions below 12 weeks of amenorrhea. Emerging epidemiologic and clinical data further question the necessity of RhD testing and provision of IgG anti‐D in cases of first‐trimester abortion due to small or non‐existant amounts of fetal RBCs and consequently the minimal risk of maternal‐fetal hemorrhage. Challenges such as limited supply, cost considerations, and accessibility issues are mentioned, albeit less frequently, but remain pertinent concerns for patient care (Table ). We assessed the risk of bias in the included studies and identified a moderate risk, compounded by methodologic limitations such as retrospective data collection and a lack of randomization. 4 DISCUSSION 4.1 Findings and interpretation Over the past decades, the gestational age at which abortions occur has significantly decreased in most countries. This shift has heightened the need for evidence‐based guidelines regarding the necessity and effectiveness of administering anti‐D immunoglobulin during first‐trimester abortions. The present study provides a comprehensive overview of the current debate worldwide, analyzing the latest guidelines from various international and national health bodies. This analysis reveals significant variability in evidence‐based recommendations across countries and organizations. Although the latest international guidelines from WHO, the US organization NAF, and the Italian National Institute of Health recommend that RhD testing and subsequent anti‐D prophylaxis is not necessary for women undergoing first‐trimester abortion, many older guidelines published before 2022 advocate for its implementation during the first trimester. The recommended gestational age for administering IgG anti‐D to RhD‐negative women undergoing abortion varies even more. Several European countries, including Austria, the Netherlands, Germany, and Ireland, recommend anti‐D prophylaxis for RhD‐negative women undergoing first‐trimester abortions, with gestational age cut‐offs ranging from under 6 weeks of amenorrhea (Austria) to over 12 weeks of amenorrhea. Other national guidelines from Spain, the Czech Republic, France, and Canada recommend anti‐D prophylaxis for all RhD‐negative women, regardless of gestational age. In contrast, national guidelines published from 2022 onwards, including the ones from the UK (RCOG) and Italy (only for medical procedures), suggest anti‐D prophylaxis for RhD‐negative women only at a gestational age above 12 weeks of amenorrhea. Notably, since the research conducted for this review, Sweden (Swedish Federation of Obstetrics and Gynecology [SFOG]), France (French National College of Gynecologists and Obstetricians [CNGOF]), and the USA (American Congress of Obstetricians and Gynecologists [ACOG]) have issued similar recommendations in 2024. Different recommendations in

from Spain, the Czech Republic, France, and Canada recommend anti‐D prophylaxis for all RhD‐negative women, regardless of gestational age. In contrast, national guidelines published from 2022 onwards, including the ones from the UK (RCOG) and Italy (only for medical procedures), suggest anti‐D prophylaxis for RhD‐negative women only at a gestational age above 12 weeks of amenorrhea. Notably, since the research conducted for this review, Sweden (Swedish Federation of Obstetrics and Gynecology [SFOG]), France (French National College of Gynecologists and Obstetricians [CNGOF]), and the USA (American Congress of Obstetricians and Gynecologists [ACOG]) have issued similar recommendations in 2024. Different recommendations in evidence‐based guidelines have also been observed in the review by Sperling et al., published in 2018, which compared four national guidelines on the prevention of RhD alloimmunization including ACOG, RCOG, the Society of Obstetricians and Gynecologists of Canada (SOGC), and The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (RANZCOG). Authors noticed variations in recommendations, particularly concerning the timing of administration, the necessity of consent, prophylaxis for specific scenarios like threatened abortion and molar pregnancy, and the use of fetal RHD genotype testing. The variability in first‐trimester abortion management can be attributed to several factors, including varying interpretations of the scarce evidence, resource availability, cultural and social factors, legal and regulatory considerations, and evolving evidence. Indeed, the literature presents diverse arguments and evidence supporting and opposing the use of IgG anti‐D during first‐trimester abortion. Proponents cite the historical success of this practice in reducing the incidence of RhD alloimmunization in European countries, preventing RhD alloimmunization and associated risks for future pregnancies, and findings from a systematic review by WHO referring to two studies from the 1970s indicating fewer instances of antibody formation in those administered IgG anti‐D before 12 weeks of gestation, with no reported adverse effects. On the other hand, arguments against routine use are based on the low amount or even absence of fetal RBCs in early pregnancy and consequently the lack of any evidence for RhD alloimmunization occurring at early gestational ages. This consideration is supported by findings of a negligible risk of alloimmunization for RhD‐negative women with spontaneous abortion before 10 weeks of amenorrhea. Despite the limited clinical evidence available, the study by Wiebe et al., published in 2019, has helped to refute the need for IgG anti‐D treatment in early pregnancy. This study compared RhD alloimmunization rates between Canada and The Netherlands. The Netherlands recommends anti‐D IgG for RhD‐negative women only after 10 weeks (spontaneous abortions) or 7 weeks (induced abortions), whereas Canada recommends it for all RhD‐negative women regardless of gestational age. The results revealed a statistically lower prevalence of antibodies in The Netherlands compared with Canada. This evidence was used by WHO guidelines to recommend anti‐D prophylaxis only for RhD‐negative women with a gestational age of 12 weeks or more of amenorrhea. Based on these findings, the Scientific Committee emphasizes the necessity of aligning with the WHO guidelines regarding the administration of anti‐D prophylaxis. The Committee members do not recommend the administration of IgG anti‐D in cases of early medical, surgical, and missed abortions below 12 weeks of amenorrhea. However, based on caution, giving IgG anti‐D to unsensitized RhD‐negative women is still recommended for abortion 12 weeks or longer of amenorrhea. Moreover, various considerations related to IgG anti‐D administration have been reported by the experts, including the human origin and therefore strict indication, its status as a precious blood product with high associated costs, the potential for allergic reactions, its impact on women, and the need for reorganization within medical services (such as appointment scheduling and access). These factors represent significant barriers for both women and medical staff and warrant careful consideration in decision making processes. These considerations are particularly relevant for medical abortion, which is an entirely noninvasive procedure. Avoiding the need for blood typing and potentially injecting IgG offers a great relief to both patients and providers. Additionally, it gives women more flexibility as to where and when to take the abortion tablets if anti‐D is no longer a concern. A recent survey conducted in 2024 also confirms these findings. This international study involving 232 abortion providers from 60 different countries collected the real‐life practice of IgG anti‐D prophylaxis in RhD‐negative women undergoing first‐trimester abortion. The results revealed major discrepancies in guidelines and practice between countries, with most providers wishing to adjust their handling of anti‐D prophylaxis based on clinical evidence and recommendations. 4.2 Expert opinion The comprehensive analysis of RhD practices reveals significant differences in evidence‐based guidelines worldwide. The latest WHO abortion guidelines, which recommend anti‐D prophylaxis only for RhD‐negative women at a gestational age of 12 weeks or more, are supported by emerging evidence and practical considerations. Notably, the study by Wiebe et al. in 2019 demonstrated lower alloimmunization rates in The Netherlands, where prophylaxis is limited

in RhD‐negative women undergoing first‐trimester abortion. The results revealed major discrepancies in guidelines and practice between countries, with most providers wishing to adjust their handling of anti‐D prophylaxis based on clinical evidence and recommendations. 4.2 Expert opinion The comprehensive analysis of RhD practices reveals significant differences in evidence‐based guidelines worldwide. The latest WHO abortion guidelines, which recommend anti‐D prophylaxis only for RhD‐negative women at a gestational age of 12 weeks or more, are supported by emerging evidence and practical considerations. Notably, the study by Wiebe et al. in 2019 demonstrated lower alloimmunization rates in The Netherlands, where prophylaxis is limited to later gestational ages, compared with Canada. Horvath et al. in 2022 further support the safety of withholding IgG anti‐D from RhD‐negative women, as the estimated fetal RBC levels may be below the threshold for maternal Rh sensitization. These findings highlight that administration of IgG anti‐D may not be necessary in early pregnancy and this can reduce unnecessary medical interventions, associated costs as well as administrative hurdles. Aligning with the WHO guidelines promotes an evidence‐based approach, minimizing potential risks for women and ensuring effective use of resources. 4.3 Strengths and weaknesses The present study demonstrates several strengths, including a rigorous methodology validated by a Prospero protocol for a systematic review. It comprehensively includes high‐quality publications, such as numerous national and international official guidelines ( n = 27), reviews ( n = 8), including a Cochrane review, and various other studies ( n = 9), providing a complete overview on the subject. Some of the included studies had substantial sample sizes, such as a cohort study with 506 patients who underwent medical or procedural abortions. Most of the studies were recently published, with the highest proportion (18%) from 2022, offering an updated and recent overview of RhD practices in first‐trimester abortion worldwide. However, the present study also has some limitations. Some of the included studies have a moderate risk of biases with low sample sizes, particularly one survey that included only 20 individuals. A review included only two trials evaluating anti‐D administration to women who underwent abortion out of 13 randomized controlled trials, and a retrospective study included 138 patients. The guidelines analyzed were generally based on studies with low levels of evidence in the context of abortion. When guidelines mention the level of evidence, they all indicate a moderate or low level (Grade B or C), derived from randomized clinical trials with important limitations or observational studies and case series. The guidelines acknowledge that further research could change the conclusions of these studies, highlighting the need for more robust evidence in this area. 4.4 Similarities and differences in relation to other studies To our knowledge, the only systematic review on anti‐D prophylaxis management in first‐trimester abortion, conducted with a European Scientific Committee, was published in 2021. None of the studies identified in the authors' search were included, meaning the NICE consensus guidelines were based solely on the clinical expertise of the guideline committee. 4.5 Open questions and future research Our findings underscore the ongoing debate surrounding anti‐D prophylaxis during first‐trimester abortion and the need to balance its potential benefits against the associated risks, as well as practical and ethical considerations. We recommend that future research focuses on comparing the incidence of RhD alloimmunization before and after the implementation of guidelines that advise against routinely administering anti‐D to Rh‐negative women undergoing first‐trimester abortion. 5 CONCLUSIONS Guidelines issued after 2022 generally do not recommend routine anti‐D prophylaxis for first‐trimester abortion (<12 weeks of amenorrhea), regardless of the method, mainly because of a lack of evidence supporting the effectiveness of IgG anti‐D administration in early abortion. The discrepancies among evidence‐based guidelines and the nuanced underlying considerations, underscore the importance of rigorous evidence appraisal, contextual awareness, and patient‐centered decision making when deciding on RhD‐typing and IgG anti‐D prophylaxis in early abortion care. Prioritizing patient safety, accessibility, and cost‐effectiveness in protocol management is essential. Standardizing protocols globally while accommodating local contexts and individual patient needs is paramount. Continuous research and collaboration are essential to establish evidence‐based guidelines and address current practice gaps. Hence, ongoing discussions and collaboration among healthcare providers and policy makers are crucial to ensure that anti‐D prophylaxis during first‐trimester abortion aligns with patient‐centered principles and advances in medical knowledge. documents.title: BSH guideline diagnosis and management of anemia of chronic disease

chunks.content: Hypoxia inducible factor (HIF) is a key transcription factor primarily involved in the cellular regulation and efficiency of oxygen delivery. Its preliminary state comprises a constitutively expressed, nucleus‐bound β‐subunit and three isoforms of a cytoplasmic α‐subunit (HIF‐1α, HIF‐2α and HIF‐3α). HIF‐1α and HIF‐2α are master regulators of defensive mechanisms against hypoxia and enhance oxygen delivery by stimulating a variety of genes. Representative target genes are erythropoietin (EPO) and those that optimize iron utilization. When oxygen availability is normal, the α‐subunit is sequentially degraded: first by prolyl hydroxylation by HIF‐prolyl hydroxylase (HIF‐PH), followed by ubiquitination via the Von‐Hippel Lindau (VHL) gene and the E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, which facilitates proteosomal degradation. However, prolyl hydroxylation is oxygen‐dependent; hence, during periods of hypoxia HIF‐PH loses its activity, resulting in stabilization of the α‐subunit before it undergoes nuclear translocation and formation of a heterodimer with the β‐subunit. As the oxygen sensing mechanism and the adaptive response against hypoxia is so important and essential, three great scientists who elucidated this mechanism, Peter Ratcliffe, Gregg Semenza, and William Kaelin Jr., were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology and Medicine in 2019. The current standard‐of‐care treatments for anaemia in chronic kidney disease (CKD) is intravenous (IV) or subcutaneous (SC) administration of human recombinant EPO or its derivatives, known as erythropoiesis stimulating agents (ESA) which stimulate the haematopoietic system specifically. HIF‐PH inhibitors (HIF‐PHI) are now approved and available in some countries as an oral drug of a completely new mechanism to treat anaemia in CKD. , , , HIF‐PHI work systemically and may exert some effects outside the haematopoietic system. Being a relatively novel therapy that was first approved in various Asia‐Pacific countries, it is important for nephrologists and clinicians within the region to well understand the potential benefits and harms when prescribing this class of drug. Based on these backgrounds, the Asian Pacific Society of Nephrology HIF‐PHI Recommendation Committee, formed by a panel of 11 nephrologists who have clinical experience or been investigators in HIF‐PHI studies, reviewed and deliberated on the current clinical and pre‐clinical evidence regarding HIF‐PHI. This Recommendation summarizes the consensus views of the Committee regarding the use of HIF‐PHI, taking into account both the available data and expert opinion in areas where evidence remains to be sought, and will be further updated when new clinical data emerges in the future. 1 RECOMMENDATIONS ON THE USE OF <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">HIF‐PHI</styled-content> 1.1 Strategy when replacing <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">ESA</styled-content> with <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">HIF‐PHI</styled-content> and the other way around <Recommendation> Physicians can consider HIF‐PHI as alternatives to ESA in correcting and maintaining haemoglobin level for renal anaemia both in dialysis‐dependent and non‐dialysis‐dependent CKD patients based on the new data concerning its efficacy and safety. Physician can consider HIF‐PHI as alternatives to ESAs in correcting and maintaining haemoglobin (Hb) for renal anaemia both in dialysis‐dependent (DD) and non‐dialysis‐dependent (NDD) CKD patients based on the new data concerning its efficacy and safety from several recent clinical trials. , These trials show that the efficacy and safety of HIF‐PHI are comparable to ESAs in treating renal anaemia in the short term, although the long‐term risks and benefits of HIF‐PHIs in treating renal anaemia remains to be assessed. Physicians should recognize that HIF‐PHI are very different in its mechanism of action of erythropoiesis compared to ESAs. ESAs stimulate erythropoiesis by acting specifically on the erythropoietin receptor that expressed on red blood cell precursors. , HIF‐PHI not only enhances erythropoietin production but also exerts other on‐target effects through many genes under the HIF pathway in all cells. These on‐target effects are influenced by pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic properties, dosing intervals and the selectivity of each inhibitor against the three different HIF‐PH enzymes. Thus, physicians should also appreciate that small molecular compounds of HIF‐PHI are likely to have some off‐target activities against structurally related enzymes because HIF‐PH enzymes are a part of a large enzyme superfamily with many important functions. Physicians should understand the pharmacologic profiles (Table ) of each HIF‐PHI based on clinical trial data, , , , , , , initiate HIF‐PHI at an appropriate dose, and adjust HIF‐PHI to achieve the Hb target stipulated in the guidelines of each country. 1.2 Supplementation of iron and monitoring of iron status <Recommendation> Iron status should be evaluated before HIF‐PHI are used. We suggest correcting iron deficiency before initiation of HIF‐PHI (ferritin > 100 ng/mL and TSAT > 20%) for all CKD patients. The iron status should be evaluated before HIF‐PHI is commenced. Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation (TSAT) are used to assess iron status, and ferritin levels <100 ng/mL [< 200 ng/mL in haemodialysis (HD) patients] or TSAT<20% are considered as iron deficiency. During induction phase of HIF‐PHI treatment (about 8 weeks), reduced TSAT occurs because of increased transferrin levels (total iron binding capacity, TIBC) and may not indicate iron deficiency. The optimal ferritin and TSAT

evaluated before HIF‐PHI are used. We suggest correcting iron deficiency before initiation of HIF‐PHI (ferritin > 100 ng/mL and TSAT > 20%) for all CKD patients. The iron status should be evaluated before HIF‐PHI is commenced. Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation (TSAT) are used to assess iron status, and ferritin levels <100 ng/mL [< 200 ng/mL in haemodialysis (HD) patients] or TSAT<20% are considered as iron deficiency. During induction phase of HIF‐PHI treatment (about 8 weeks), reduced TSAT occurs because of increased transferrin levels (total iron binding capacity, TIBC) and may not indicate iron deficiency. The optimal ferritin and TSAT levels in the maintenance phase of HIF‐PHI treatment remain undefined, and in this context we suggest ferritin levels of no less than 100 ng/mL and TSAT no less than 20% (opinion). Iron deficiency should be corrected before initiation of HIF‐PHI (ferritin>100 ng/mL and TSAT>20%) for all CKD patients. For NDD patients, we suggest using oral iron for those who require iron supplementation. For DD patients, we suggest oral iron to be tried first and IV iron be considered an alternative for those who do not tolerate oral iron or when the physician opines that IV iron is necessary. Pre‐clinical and clinical studies have shown that HIF activation is associated with enhanced intestinal iron absorption and increased availability of iron for erythropoiesis. , , , , Clinical trials showed that less IV iron was required in HIF‐PHI arm compared with ESA arm in DD patients. Phase 2 and 3 trials in China showed that the effect of roxadustat was not dependent on IV iron in both NDD and DD patients. , In clinical studies, HIF‐PHIs have been shown to increase blood TIBC with no significant changes in serum iron levels, resulting in reduced TSAT. Treatment with HIF‐PHI is also associated with decreased blood ferritin level and hepcidin level. , Iron deficiency is associated with thromboembolic events, and clinical trials of roxadustat in Japan have reported increased incidence of thromboembolic events. As treatment with HIF‐PHIs may decrease serum iron levels due to increased availability of iron for erythropoiesis, one should pay attention to avoid treatment‐induced reduction in serum iron levels. 1.3 Types of patients who should be treated with <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">HIF‐PH</styled-content> inhibitor rather than <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">ESA</styled-content> <Recommendation> Anaemia in CKD should be controlled using ESAs or HIF‐PHI after sufficient iron supplementation. If patients with good drug adherence desire oral treatment because of various reasons such as frequency of hospital visits and invasiveness of injections in case of non‐HD patients, HIF‐PHI may be preferable than ESAs. In case of treatment with HIF‐PHI, an issue of polypharmacy should be acceptable. If target Hb cannot be achieved with the recommended dose of ESA, the priority is to search for the cause of ESA hyporesponsiveness and consultation with a nephrologist/specialized medical institution should be considered. If the cause of ESA hyporesponsiveness is unknown or difficult to manage due to defective iron utilization or some other reasons, conversion to HIF‐PHI should be considered. 1.3.1 <italic toggle="yes"><styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CKD</styled-content> stage <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">G3</styled-content> ~ <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">G5</styled-content>, or <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">G5T</styled-content></italic> Anaemia in CKD stage G3 ~ 5 or G5T patients can be managed with ESAs or HIF‐PHI after sufficient iron supplementation. If patients with good drug adherence desire oral treatment because of various reasons such as frequency of hospital visits and invasiveness of injections, HIF‐PHI may be preferable than ESAs. In case of treatment with HIF‐PHI, an issue of polypharmacy should be acceptable. Patient should be screened for malignant tumour and retinal lesions before the use of HIF‐PHI. HIF‐PHI can be commenced when confirmed that there are no such complications or that appropriate treatment has been provided. It is advisable to avoid the use of HIF‐PHI when the above medical conditions are poorly controlled as the long‐term safety data are lacking. The use of HIF‐PHI should be exercised with caution in patients with pre‐existing ischemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disease or peripheral vascular disease (obstructive arteriosclerosis and deep vein thrombosis) because of the concerns of thromboembolic complications. The size of renal cysts should also be followed when HIF‐PHI is used in patients with polycystic kidney disease, as acceleration of cysts expansions by HIF‐PHI has been observed in animal studies. If the target Hb cannot be achieved with the recommended dose of ESA, the priority is to search for the cause of ESA hyporesponsiveness and consider consultation with a nephrologist/specialized medical institution. If the cause of ESA hyporesponsiveness is unknown or difficult to manage due to defective iron utilization or some other reasons, conversion to HIF‐PHI should be considered. 1.3.2 <italic toggle="yes"><styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CKD</styled-content> stage <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">G5D</styled-content></italic> Anaemia in CKD stage G5D patients should be managed with ESA or HIF‐PHI after adequate iron supplementation. In patients receiving peritoneal dialysis (PD), HIF‐PHI may be preferred to ESA

in animal studies. If the target Hb cannot be achieved with the recommended dose of ESA, the priority is to search for the cause of ESA hyporesponsiveness and consider consultation with a nephrologist/specialized medical institution. If the cause of ESA hyporesponsiveness is unknown or difficult to manage due to defective iron utilization or some other reasons, conversion to HIF‐PHI should be considered. 1.3.2 <italic toggle="yes"><styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">CKD</styled-content> stage <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">G5D</styled-content></italic> Anaemia in CKD stage G5D patients should be managed with ESA or HIF‐PHI after adequate iron supplementation. In patients receiving peritoneal dialysis (PD), HIF‐PHI may be preferred to ESA especially in those with good drug compliance and desire oral therapy to minimize the frequency of hospital visits and avoid parenteral drug administration. As in CKD G3 ~ 5 or G5T patients, an issue of polypharmacy should be acceptable. The concerns and precautions for malignancy, retinal tumour, thromboembolic events and cyst growth (in patients with polycystic kidney disease) are similar to that in CKD G3‐5 or G5T patients. Acquired cystic disease of the kidney in DD patients is prone to develop malignancy, and one should monitor for the development of tumour in patients with acquired cystic disease of the kidney treated with HIF‐PHI. As in CKD G3 ~ 5 or G5T patients, clinicians should first investigate for the cause of ESA hyporesponsiveness and consider consulting a dialysis specialist/specialized medical institution if the Hb level cannot be achieved with the recommended dose of ESA. Conversion to HIF‐PHI should be considered if the cause of ESA hyporesponsiveness is unknown or difficult to manage due to defective iron utilization or some other reasons. 2 POTENTIAL CONCERNS OF <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">HIF‐PHI</styled-content> 2.1 Malignancy <Recommendation> Before prescribing HIF‐PHI, the presence and risk of malignancy should be ascertained and, in patients with known malignancy, administration should be undertaken only with great caution—if at all. Given the theoretical and experimental concerns associated with sustained increased HIF activity, as well as evidence of the long‐term malignancy risk posed by related genetic diseases, it will be essential to maintain post‐marketing cancer surveillance for at least 5 years. Apart from increasing EPO transcription and inhibiting hepcidin production, HIF also induces transcription of genes relating to neo‐vascularization and tumour growth (specific to tumour type). These include vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), nitric oxide, TWIST gene, metalloproteinase and mitogen‐activated protein kinase, among others. Importantly, HIF‐1α (rather than HIF‐2α) appears related to tumour gene activity and associated with metastatic spread for breast, prostate, lung, bone and colorectal cancers. Nonetheless, HIF‐2α has also been identified in in vitro malignant hepatocellular lines, is involved in the activation of cancer stem cells factor and is strongly associated with various tumour metastases, as well as a poor prognosis. , The relevance of HIF activation on the potential for malignancy is evident in conditions such as VHL disease, where the incidence of several tumours, including renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is increased. Conversely, most RCCs display somatic mutations in the VHL gene, reducing proteolysis of the HIF α‐subunit and increasing HIF activity. Solid tumours have a poorer prognosis when HIF activity is increased and trials examining the clinical effect of HIF inhibitors on RCCs are underway. Given the association between HIF and tumour progression, emergence of the HIF‐PHI forces us to consider whether stimulating HIF transcription might also raise the risk of initiating or progressing tumour growth. There are five different agents that are currently in or have recently completed Phase 3 studies: daprodustat, roxadustat, vadadustat, molidustat and enarodustat. Newer agents in development include desidustat (ZYAN1), which has recently completed a Phase 2 study in Australia, and JNJ‐429045343, which is in pre‐clinical development. Of these, roxadustat is approved for clinical use in Japan and China, and daprodustat and vadadustat are approved for clinical use in Japan. Additional applications relating to other compounds are pending. Although there is a recognised class effect, insofar as each agent selectively inhibits the prolyl hydroxylase (PHD) enzymes with reductions in serum hepcidin and ferritin and shares a similar cardiovascular profile, each has a distinct molecular structure, half‐life, adverse event profile and probably PHD selectivity. Molidustat for instance primarily inhibits PHD 2, and daprodustat PHD 2 and PHD 3, whereas roxadustat appears to inhibit all three PHDs. Whether such selectivity will influence malignancy risk for individual PHIs remains to be seen. Despite the theoretical potential for oncogenesis for any and all the PHIs, there is minimal evidence to date of such concerns—and of note that none of the phase 3 trials have been ceased by the relevant data monitoring committee. If this safety profile proves to be sustained, reasons could relate to the dominant role of HIF‐1α in tumour development and progression and the relative selectivity (particularly HIF‐2α) of the PHIs. Another possibility is the apparently small effect of PHIs on HIF activity: no trial

three PHDs. Whether such selectivity will influence malignancy risk for individual PHIs remains to be seen. Despite the theoretical potential for oncogenesis for any and all the PHIs, there is minimal evidence to date of such concerns—and of note that none of the phase 3 trials have been ceased by the relevant data monitoring committee. If this safety profile proves to be sustained, reasons could relate to the dominant role of HIF‐1α in tumour development and progression and the relative selectivity (particularly HIF‐2α) of the PHIs. Another possibility is the apparently small effect of PHIs on HIF activity: no trial has demonstrated detectable changes in serum VEGF and all have indicated only marginal increases in serum EPO concentrations. The latter is in contrast to findings from the TREAT study, where a marked increase in deaths from cancer was suggested in association with administration of the erythropoietic stimulating agent, darbepoetin. At least two agents have been assessed regarding their potential for cancer development in longer‐term murine studies: roxadustat and daprodustat. , Roxadustat is usually administered to humans at doses up to 1.5 mg/kg daily or thrice‐weekly (TIW). At doses of up to 10 (rats) and 60 (mice) mg/kg administered TIW and followed for up to 104 weeks, there was no effect in either animal on survival or on the development of neoplastic lesions. Similarly, daprodustat was administered to a cohort of mice and Sprague‐Dawley rats for up to 2 years at ≥143‐fold the predicted maximal human clinical exposure. Again, no neoplastic changes were observed, although (male) rat lifespan was curtailed due erythrocytosis, aortic thrombosis and/or associated cardiomyopathy. In summary, from the available animal and short‐term human data, so far there is no evidence of tumour risk with the use of PHIs. Whether the same can be said for humans, and whether there is a difference between primary oncogenesis and enhancing known tumour growth and spread is unclear. Some idea of the relative risk of malignancy will be available following publication of current studies, but since patients with known tumours were unlikely to be enrolled, it is probable such questions will not be fully addressed. Given broad marketing approval ensues, or in Japan maintained, it will be essential to maintain post‐marketing surveillance for a substantive period—at least 5 years—given the theoretical and experimental concerns associated with increased HIF activity, as well as the long‐term malignancy risk posed by related genetic diseases. 2.2 Retinopathy <Recommendation> Retinopathy is a theoretical concern of HIF‐PHI in CKD patients. Early referral for ophthalmologic assessment is warranted in patients who report visual disturbance after drug initiation. Retinopathy is a sight‐threatening condition and remains a serious concern in the use of HIF‐stabilizer in CKD patients. Theoretically, activation of the HIF pathway may enhance retinal angiogenesis and predispose patients to retinal complications such as haemorrhage. The overall incidence of retinal adverse events is low. While the current data suggest that HIF‐PHI is not associated with increased risk of retinal haemorrhage compared with ESA, one should appreciate that patients with high propensity for retinal complications were excluded from clinical trials of HIF‐PHI published. , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , Furthermore, duration of these clinical trials may have been too short or too small to observe aggravation of retinal adverse events. It is important to have high alertness if patient reports visual disturbance after initiation of HIF‐PHI and early referral for ophthalmologic assessment is warranted. 2.3 Liver dysfunction <Recommendation> Liver dysfunction is relatively uncommon in CKD patients receiving HIF‐PHI. Regular monitoring of liver function may facilitate early detection of HIF‐PHI ‐related hepatic dysfunction. The effect of HIF on liver and hepatic diseases remains elusive. Animal data suggest that HIF confers protective effect on ischaemic‐reperfusion injury of liver but shows pathogenic roles in the progression of hepatic fibrosis and fatty liver. In an open‐label randomized study in dialysis patients, transient elevation of liver biochemistries was noted in two roxadustat‐treated patients (3.3%) during the 12‐week treatment period and both showed normalization of liver function without drug discontinuation. In a phase 3 study of roxadustat in Chinese patients receiving dialysis, two subjects (1%) showed liver dysfunction which was mild or moderate in severity. The derangement in liver function test, however, was not observed in another phase 3 study of roxadustat conducted in NDD Chinese CKD patients. Liver dysfunction was also not reported in phase 2 or 3 studies of other HIF‐PHI including desidustat, enarodustat, molidustat and vadadustat. , , , , , , , While the incidence of hepatic abnormalities is low, regular monitoring of liver function may help facilitate early detection of HIF‐PHI‐related hepatic dysfunction. 2.4 Hyperkalemia <Recommendation> The data on hyperkalemia as an adverse effect of HIF‐PHI is inconclusive. However, considering hyperkalemia can be a medical emergency, we suggest serum potassium

The derangement in liver function test, however, was not observed in another phase 3 study of roxadustat conducted in NDD Chinese CKD patients. Liver dysfunction was also not reported in phase 2 or 3 studies of other HIF‐PHI including desidustat, enarodustat, molidustat and vadadustat. , , , , , , , While the incidence of hepatic abnormalities is low, regular monitoring of liver function may help facilitate early detection of HIF‐PHI‐related hepatic dysfunction. 2.4 Hyperkalemia <Recommendation> The data on hyperkalemia as an adverse effect of HIF‐PHI is inconclusive. However, considering hyperkalemia can be a medical emergency, we suggest serum potassium being monitored in patients receiving HIF‐PHI treatment. Among the 25 published randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluate the efficacy of HIF‐PHI on renal anaemia, , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , nine have reported hyperkalemia (Table , and Table ). Six of these studies reported a higher incidence rate of hyperkalaemia among patients treated with HIF‐PHI while the other three studies have reported increased rates of hyperkalaemia in the control arm. For NDD patients, hyperkalemia was reported as a TEAE (>5% events) in 4 of the 12 clinical studies. Three of the four roxadustat RCTs reported higher incidence rates of hyperkalemia [26/250 (10%) vs 6/109 (5.5%) in roxdustat and control groups respectively]. , , , One of two RCTs of vadadustat reported increased incidence of hyperkalemia [7/138 (5%) vs 0/72 (0%) in vadadustat and control arms respectively]. While the phase 3 study in China reported higher rate of hyperkalemia in roxadustat arm, there was no difference in hyperkalemia between roxadustat and the placebo groups when data from the central laboratory was used for analysis. As for DD patients, five out of the 13 RCTs reported hyperkalemia. Three of the four roxadustat studies reported higher rates of hyperkalemia [16/386 (4.1%) vs 3/158 (1.8%) in roxadustat and control groups respectively). , , , Two of the five daprodustat studies reported increased incidence rates of hyperkalemia [8/239 (3.3%) vs 1/59 (1.6%) in daprodustat and control groups, respectively]. , , , , As in NDD patients, the rates of hyperkalemia were comparable between roxadustat and control groups when the central laboratory data were used for analysis. Taken together, although higher rates of hyperkalemia have been reported in the HIF‐PHI arm in some studies, the data so far remain inconclusive. Considering that hyperkalemia can be a life‐threatening complication, we suggest that serum potassium being monitored after the initiation of HIF‐PHI and regularly during the treatment. 2.5 Hypertension <Recommendation> Clinical studies have no signals that suggest a hypertensive effect of HIF‐PHI, but as ESA use is associated with hypertension or compromised blood pressure control, one should pay attention to blood pressure control in patients treated with HIF‐PHI. It is well recognized that the administration of ESA is associated with development of hypertension and compromised blood pressure control. Therefore, the effect of HIF‐PHI on blood pressure has been a valid concern. While some pre‐clinical data have suggested that HIF‐PHIs may have anti‐hypertensive effect, clinical studies so far also have no signals that suggest hypertensive effect of HIF‐PHI , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , (Table and Table ) Furthermore, there is by far no studies that specifically examines the effect of HIF‐PHI on blood pressure in humans. 2.6 Pulmonary hypertension and heart failure <Recommendation> Clinical studies have no signals that suggest aggravation of pulmonary hypertension or heart failure by HIF‐PHI, but one should pay attention to changes of cardiac function in patients treated with HIF‐PHI. Pulmonary hypertension and heart failure are common cardiovascular complications among CKD patients. It was reported that pulmonary hypertension and heart failure were present in 30%‐40% and 40%‐59% of patients with CKD respectively, , , and the prevalence increases with the more advanced stages of CKD. Studies on genetic HIF activation, for example, Chuvash polycythaemia, which is caused by homozygous mutation of VHL, reported that severe pulmonary hypertension may occur in this hypoxia sensing disorder. , Studies using viable heterozygous HIF‐2alpha‐deficient mice after exposure to hypoxia showed protection against pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular hypertrophy in HIF‐2α‐deficient mice, unveiling a critical role of HIF‐2α in hypoxia‐induced pulmonary vascular remodelling. HIF‐2α was shown to mediate upregulation of vasoconstrictors which contribute to the development of hypoxic pulmonary vascular remodelling. Further, inactivation of Phd2 in endothelial cells resulted in severe pulmonary hypertension, abnormal muscularization of peripheral pulmonary arteries, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Concurrent inactivation of either Hif1a or Hif2a in endothelial cell‐specific Phd2 mutants demonstrated that the development of pulmonary hypertension was dependent on HIF‐2α but not HIF‐1α. Persistent HIF activation may cause more intense vasoconstrictive effect to hypoxia at pulmonary vasculatures leading to increased pulmonary pressure. The potential adverse effect of aggravating pulmonary

role of HIF‐2α in hypoxia‐induced pulmonary vascular remodelling. HIF‐2α was shown to mediate upregulation of vasoconstrictors which contribute to the development of hypoxic pulmonary vascular remodelling. Further, inactivation of Phd2 in endothelial cells resulted in severe pulmonary hypertension, abnormal muscularization of peripheral pulmonary arteries, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Concurrent inactivation of either Hif1a or Hif2a in endothelial cell‐specific Phd2 mutants demonstrated that the development of pulmonary hypertension was dependent on HIF‐2α but not HIF‐1α. Persistent HIF activation may cause more intense vasoconstrictive effect to hypoxia at pulmonary vasculatures leading to increased pulmonary pressure. The potential adverse effect of aggravating pulmonary hypertension by HIF‐PHIs, however, has not been reported in recently published RCTs. , Correction of renal anaemia has been shown to reduce incidence of heart failure and improve cardiac function. However, there were a series of reports on reduced cardiac function following sustained activation of HIF or inhibition of prolyl hydroxylase. , , , Studies of HIF deletion in a model of heart failure reported discrepant results. , The molecular mechanism of this effect is not clearly defined. Basic science studies suggested that this might be associated with the extent of HIF activation, where over‐activation of HIF might lead to defective energy utilisation of the cardiac myocytes. This highlights the importance of the fine balance between prolyl hydroxylase inhibition to stimulate erythropoiesis for correction of renal anaemia and modest HIF activation at the heart to prevent deterioration of cardiac function. One should also pay attention to the experimental study which showed that HIF‐1 directly up‐regulated BNP, a marker of heart failure. The potential benefits of HIF‐PHIs on improving myocardial ischaemia and the potential risks of compromising cardiac function need to be further studied in RCTs. 2.7 Thrombotic events and vascular calcification <Recommendation> Clinical data and basic studies raise the concerns of thrombotic events in HIF‐PHI treatment. We suggest a limited use of HIF‐PH inhibitors in patients with any history of thrombotic events or a careful use of HIF‐PHI in patients with cardiovascular disease. Large studies with unbiased reports and long‐term follow‐up are required. 2.7.1 <italic toggle="yes">Concerns from ESA trials and patients with HIF pathway mutations</italic> Previous studies have demonstrated that treatment of anaemia in CKD by ESAs increases Hb levels, reduce transfusion requirements and improves quality of life. , , However, treatment to high Hb targets with large doses of ESA has resulted in increased rates of vascular access thrombosis, cerebrovascular events, cardiovascular events and mortality. , Patients with mutations in genes such as VHL, EGLN1 (encoding PHD2), EPAS1 (encoding HIF2α), and the EPO receptor can result in polycythemia and vascular complications such as cerebral vascular events and peripheral thromboembolism. , The lessons from ESA trials and patients with HIF pathway mutations imply the thrombotic risk of HIF‐PH inhibitor treatment. Whether this is an issue in patients with reasonable Hb target and with low risk of cardiovascular disease at enrollment is not clear. 2.7.2 <italic toggle="yes">Concerns from basic studies</italic> Basic studies have shown that HIF pathway is associated with thrombosis and plaque stability. In this context, hypoxia and HIF target genes modulate coagulation, fibrinolysis, and thrombus resolution. HIF increases tissue factor expression and triggers thrombus formation. Other important biological effects include suppression of anti‐coagulating factors (eg, tissue factor pathway inhibitor and protein S) and also increase in plasminogen activator inhibitor 1, which in turn inhibits fibrinolysis. , Plaque stability is related to the expression of HIF within the plaque, specifically its expression in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), endothelial cells (ECs) and more importantly foam cells. HIF can also stimulate destabilised angiogenesis occurring in the ischaemic and necrotic atherosclerotic lesion. HIF and HIF‐induced genes, especially VEGF, can enhance the haemodynamic instability and fragility of the plaque, thus allows further infiltration of inflammatory cells. , Basic studies have also shown that HIF pathway may be associated with atherosclerosis and vascular calcification. Atherosclerosis involves endothelial activation, lipid accumulation, foam cell formation and VSMCs proliferation. HIF‐1 and its associated products such as NF‐kB, VEGF and NO cause EC dysfunction, proliferation, angiogenesis and inflammation. HIF‐1 and its product such as ET‐1 and MIF, together with cytokines from activated ECs could induce VSMC migration and proliferation. HIF‐1 causes migration and inflammation of macrophage with M1 phenotype differentiation, which produces inflammatory cytokines and promotes the formation of foam cells. , However, some studies showed the possible benefits of HIF activation through cholesterol metabolism or inhibiting antigen‐presenting cell activation. Vascular calcification involves osteochondrogenic differentiation of VSMCs. HIF‐1 and the upregulated RUNX2 and OCN contribute to hypoxia‐mediated osteochondrogenic differentiation and extracellular matrix calcification in VSMCs. 2.7.3 <italic toggle="yes">Concerns from HIF‐PH inhibitor clinical trials</italic> We reviewed published placebo or competitor‐controlled trials of six HIF‐PH inhibitors in DD and NDD CKD patients. The pooled incidence of thrombotic side effects by HIF‐PHI according to the status of CKD status were summarized

phenotype differentiation, which produces inflammatory cytokines and promotes the formation of foam cells. , However, some studies showed the possible benefits of HIF activation through cholesterol metabolism or inhibiting antigen‐presenting cell activation. Vascular calcification involves osteochondrogenic differentiation of VSMCs. HIF‐1 and the upregulated RUNX2 and OCN contribute to hypoxia‐mediated osteochondrogenic differentiation and extracellular matrix calcification in VSMCs. 2.7.3 <italic toggle="yes">Concerns from HIF‐PH inhibitor clinical trials</italic> We reviewed published placebo or competitor‐controlled trials of six HIF‐PH inhibitors in DD and NDD CKD patients. The pooled incidence of thrombotic side effects by HIF‐PHI according to the status of CKD status were summarized in Table and 4B. , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , , In DD patients, the incidence of CV events was low (42/1741 [2.4%]). HIF‐PH inhibitors were associated with higher incidence of all‐cause mortality, hyperkalemia and CV events (Table ). In NDD patients, the incidence of CV events was even lower (21/1871 [1.1%]). HIF‐PHI were associated with insignificantly higher incidence of all‐cause mortality, hyperkalaemia and CV events (Table ). Notwithstanding, one should be aware of the limitations of these pooled data. First, all the clinical trials excluded patients with any history or ‘recent’ history of thrombotic events (acute coronary syndrome, stroke, or a thromboembolic event) although the exclusion criteria vary between different trials. Second, the duration of treatment was short, which could underestimate the incidence and long‐term impact on thrombotic complications. Third, the dose and interval vary between trials despite the target Hb was reasonable in all the trials. Fourth, some side effects might not be well‐reported in these clinical trials. Previous ESA trials and basic studies have raised concerns of thrombotic events in HIF‐PHI treatment. Indeed, pooled data from clinical trials of HIF‐PHI still implies the risk for thrombotic events when high‐risk patients have already been excluded from these studies. Large studies with unbiased reports of side effects and long‐term follow‐up are eagerly awaited. At present, we suggest a careful use of HIF‐PHI in DD CKD patients with low CV risk and a restricted off‐label use in CKD patients with high CV risk. 2.8 Cyst growth <Recommendation> One should follow sizes of cysts up when HIF‐PHI are used in patients with polycystic kidney disease. Both HIF‐1α and HIF‐2α are scarcely detectable in normal kidneys. However, systemic and regional hypoxia result in stabilization of HIF‐1α in tubular epithelial cells and of HIF‐2α in peritubular and glomerular cells. Polycystic kidneys are characterized by chronic stabilization of HIF in cyst lining epithelial and peritubular interstitial cells. This is mainly due to regional hypoxia as a consequence of compression by enlarged cysts and a mismatch between expanding cysts and the vascularization of cyst walls, but not the genetic defects. Data from animal models further support this idea. Tissue PO 2 in cortical surface of Lewis polycystic kidney rats is approximately half of that in control rats. Moreover, renal blood flow and oxygen delivery in the polycystic rats are 60% and 80% lower than control rats. Overproduction of EPO by increased HIF‐2α in chronic hypoxia may explain why patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) present with less severe anaemia than patients with other end‐stage kidney disease (ESKD). Indeed, serum levels of EPO in ESKD patients due to ADPKD are on average 2‐fold higher than in ESKD of other causes. However, the stabilization of HIF in the polycystic disease confers not only such beneficial outcome but also deleterious effects in cyst enlargement. Recent study with mouse ADPKD models in combination with genetic and pharmacological approaches clearly demonstrated that increased levels of HIF‐1α due to chronic hypoxia promote cyst progression. HIF‐1α‐dependent apical Ca2 + ‐activated Cl − secretion is known as a major driving force for cyst fluid secretion. This study also identified the Ca 2+ ‐activated Cl‐channel ‘anoctamin 1’ and the purinergic receptor ‘P2Y2R’ as 2 major molecular players in the HIF‐1α‐mediated cyst growth. Although the erythropoietic dosage of a HIF‐PHI for CKD patients might be different from that used for the animal experiments, undesirable action of HIF‐1α on cyst expansion should be taken into consideration in long‐term administration of HIF‐PHI to treat anaemia in ADPKD patients. 2.9 Seizure or neurological complications <Recommendation> Clinical studies have no signals that suggest seizure or neurological complications as an adverse event by HIF‐PHI. HIF is involved in transcriptional responses to hypoxia of many genes, and hence its systemic effect on the cerebrovascular system is of potential concern. In theory, HIF‐PHI may increase thromboembolic events or seizures but very few cerebrovascular events have been reported in the clinical studies. One should appreciate that all of these clinical trials have relatively short duration of follow‐up and further studies are needed for the evaluation of these potential side effects. Clinical studies have no signals that suggest seizure or neurological complications as an adverse event by HIF‐PHI. HIF is involved in transcriptional responses to hypoxia of many genes, and hence its systemic effect on the cerebrovascular system is of potential concern. In theory, HIF‐PHI may increase thromboembolic events or seizures but very few cerebrovascular events have been reported in the clinical studies. One should appreciate that all of these clinical trials have relatively short duration of follow‐up and further studies are needed for the evaluation of these potential side effects. Studies on roxadustat in NDD patients have reported dizziness and headache , but not stroke or seizure. , In DD (including both HD and PD) populations, headache (but not stroke or seizure) had been reported in patients treated with roxadustat. In a US study, cerebrovascular accident (1.9%) and complex partial seizure (0.9%) occurred after 19 weeks of roxadustat in ESKD patients receiving maintenance HD, and such adverse events were not observed in the epoetin alfa group. Cerebral infarction (0.7%) was also reported in a study of Japanese population after 24 weeks treatment with roxadustat compared to none in the darbopoietin alfa group. One study reported that vadadustat treatment in NDD CKD patients was associated with slightly higher incidence of headache and dizziness compared with placebo during the 20 weeks of treatment. Headache was also more common in NDD CKD patients treated with daprodustat for 1 month compared with placebo, although adverse cerebrovascular event did not occur in another study where NDD patients had received 4 weeks of daprodustat. There was no cerebrovascular adverse events or stroke reported In CKD stage 3 to 5 NDD patients treated with molidustat for 16 weeks. , 3 POTENTIAL BENEFITS IN ADDITION TO IMPROVEMENT OF ANAEMIA One potential benefits of HIF‐PHI is that HIF‐PHI may stimulate erythropoiesis by an increase in circulating EPO levels within a physiological range. However, many clinical studies did not employ time points at which circulating EPO levels reach the peak by administration of HIF‐PHI. As hypoxia is a final common pathway to ESKD, HIF‐PHI may preserve kidney function in CKD patients. , , , In addition, HIF is a master regulator of defensive mechanisms against hypoxia, HIF‐PHI may provide protection against ischaemic diseases such as ischemic heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease and acute kidney injury. , , However, there is no solid clinical evidence to support these expectations, and clinical studies to clarify these issues are awaited. Previous clinical trials showed a decrease in lipids after HIF‐PHI treatment. However, treatment with HIF‐PHI decreased both LDL‐cholesterol and HDL‐cholesterol in these trials. In addition, while some HIF‐PHI showed lipid‐lowering effects, others did not. Therefore, this effect may be agent specific, and long‐term consequences of metabolic changes induced by HIF‐PHI remain to be elucidated.
